title: Who’s on Our Shelf?
objective: Students will count who is on their own class shelf, using the *Who’s in your books?* survey, and turn the count into fractions, percents and a bar graph. They will set their percent beside the Cooperative Children’s Book Center’s 2025 figures, and ask whether one shelf is a fair sample of all books.

objectives.heading: By the end of this lesson you will be able to:
objectives.why: Numbers can show who is in the books we read, and who is missing. Counting our own shelf, and asking whether it is a fair sample, is how a mathematician checks a claim before believing it.

materials: *Who Do You See?*, *Who’s in your books?* tab (online), projected
One book with a main character for each student; calculators
Page 3 of this plan; differentiated handouts
questions: Who did you find the most of? Who was hardest to find?
Which books would you add to make your shelf look more like the world?
The CCBC counted books published in 2025. Our shelf has books from many years. Does that matter?
Poster 2 calls the first Black Barbie a milestone in representation. What would a milestone look like on our shelf?
questionsLabel: Questions to ask in front of the posters
connection: **Online,** the *Who’s in your books?* tab counts the hands, draws the chart and prints it, and can count toys, shows and games as well as books. **In the exhibition,** count the dolls in the display case.

steps.title: Make a guess
script: Ask: *“Guess: of every 100 children’s books published in 2025, how many were about Black/African people?”* Students write a guess and say what it is based on.

screen.question: Guess: of every 100 children’s books published in 2025, how many were about Black/African people?

steps.purpose: Guess before being told, so the real figure means something.
students: What is your guess based on?

steps.title: Books published in 2025
script: Show the Cooperative Children’s Book Center’s figures as the room gives them (page 3). A percent is a rate per hundred: 13.5% means 13.5 out of every 100. Ask whose guess was higher and whose was lower, then: *what is the difference between a book* about *Black/African people and one* by *a Black/African author or illustrator?* Read the figures, but don’t calculate with them: the CCBC asks to review any analysis of its data.

screen.text: Of the 3,638 children’s and young adult books published in 2025 that the Cooperative Children’s Book Center received, 491 (13.5%) were about Black/African people, and 398 (10.9%) were by Black/African authors or illustrators.
screen.cite: Cooperative Children’s Book Center, University of Wisconsin–Madison

steps.purpose: Read a real percent, and what it counts.
students: Was your guess higher or lower?
What is the difference between a book *about* and a book *by*?

steps.title: Count, fraction, percent
script: Work the timeline’s numbers (page 3). The *Black Barbie Timeline* has 8 stops, and 5 of them quote poster 2: 5/8, and 5 ÷ 8 × 100 = 62.5%. Kitty Black Perkins designed the dolls at 2 of the 8 stops, the first Black Barbie in 1980 and Shani in 1991: 2 ÷ 8 × 100 = 25%. Students check: 3 stops are museum notes, 3/8 = 37.5%.

examples.title: A fraction
steps: The Black Barbie Timeline has 8 stops
examples.answer: 5/8 of the stops quote the poster

examples.title: A percent
examples.answer: 62.5% of the stops quote the poster

examples.title: Another part
steps: Kitty Black Perkins designed the dolls at 2 of the 8 stops: 1980 and Shani, 1991

steps.purpose: Turn a count into a fraction and a percent, with the timeline’s own numbers.
students: How many of the 8 stops are museum notes? What percent is that?

steps.title: Our survey
script: Open *Who’s in your books?* and run the **Background** question: read each choice, count the hands, and set the count. Run **Authors** too, and **Gender** or **Disability** if there is time. Students copy the Background and Authors counts onto their handouts. The total is the number of books.

screen.caption: Who’s in your books? The survey’s four questions

cells: Hands up if the main character in your book is…

steps.purpose: Count our own shelf, one question at a time.
students: Hold your book. Put your hand up once, for one choice.
Why does every question have a *Can’t tell*?

steps.title: A fair sample?
script: Ask: *“Does our shelf tell us about all children’s books?”* Our shelf is a **sample**; all children’s books are the **population**. A sample is **biased** when the way it was chosen makes some results more likely. Who chose the books on our shelf? When were they published? Ask: *what would make a sample fairer?*

screen.question: Does our shelf tell us about all children’s books?

steps.purpose: Meet the ideas of a sample and of bias.
students: Who chose the books on our shelf?
What would make a sample fairer?

steps.title: Choose a handout
script: Students choose a handout. All three use the class’s own count, so the answers are yours to check on the board.

levels.name: Green Level
levels.summary: Copy the class count into a table, write fractions and a percent, shade a bar graph, and set the shelf’s percent beside the CCBC’s.

levels.name: Yellow Level
levels.summary: Complete a frequency table with fractions and percents, graph it, compare characters and creators with the CCBC’s *about* and *by*, and say what a graph cannot show.

levels.name: Red Level
levels.summary: Decide what the whole should be when some books are *Can’t tell*, compare what each count measures, judge the sample for bias, design a fairer survey, and make a claim with evidence.

steps.purpose: Work with our own count at the right level of challenge.
students: Choose Green, Yellow or Red. All three use our class’s own count.

steps.title: Add to the shelf
script: Show the tab’s chart. Ask: *who did you find the most of? Who was hardest to find?* Then: *“Which books would you add to make your shelf look more like the world?”* Ask a Red Level student whether the shelf is a fair sample, and why.

screen.question: Which books would you add to make your shelf look more like the world?

steps.purpose: Turn the numbers into a decision.

steps.title: Look back
script: Put the objectives back on the screen, asked as questions: *“Can you now…?”* For each one, students show a thumb up, sideways or down. Ask one student to answer each aloud; for the last, ask a Red Level reader.
